readings.title: How They Broke Away to Go to the Rootabaga Country, part 1: a ticket to the sky
readings.challenge: Listen for words and lists that come back again and again.
readings.focus: A family tired of a house where nothing changes sells everything and buys a ticket to where the railroad runs into the sky.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. This is the first story in the book. Spot cash is money paid on the spot; a rag picker gathers old rags to sell; the conductor checks tickets on a train.

excerpt.locator: “How They Broke Away to Go to the Rootabaga Country,” from Gimme the Ax’s house to the Over and Under country; opens “Gimme the Ax lived in a house where everything is the same as it always was.”; closes “…Under country. Nobody gets out of the way of anybody else. They either go over or under.””.

questions.prompt: What does Gimme the Ax keep saying about his house?
facilitatorNotes: “Everything is the same as it always was”: the chimney, the doorknobs, the windows, upstairs and downstairs. His children learn to say it too.
evidence: Everything is the same as it always was.

questions.prompt: How do the children get their names?
facilitatorNotes: Their father lets the first words they speak be their names, so they are called Please Gimme and Ax Me No Questions. Children can guess what each child first said.
evidence: The first words they speak as soon as they learn to make words shall be their names

questions.prompt: What do they sell, and why do you think Sandburg says the list three times?
facilitatorNotes: Pigs, pastures, pepper pickers, pitchforks. The p-sounds are fun to say, and repeating the list makes it sound like a chant or a song.
evidence: pigs, pastures, pepper pickers, pitchforks

questions.prompt: What kind of ticket does the ticket agent give them? Why does Gimme the Ax look at it so often?
facilitatorNotes: A long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it. It is new and strange, and it is his only way to the place he has sold everything to reach. “Spanch” is a made-up word; ask what children picture.
evidence: a long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it

questions.prompt: The family says, “It is too much to be too long anywhere.” Do you agree? Why might they want to leave?
facilitatorNotes: Their life never changes, and they want something new. Some children will want to stay where things are familiar; others will love the idea of setting off. Both are fair.
evidence: It is too much to be too long anywhere

readings.title: How They Broke Away, part 2: balloons, clowns and pigs with bibs
readings.challenge: Picture each strange country the train passes, one at a time.
readings.focus: The train passes the balloon pickers and the clown ovens and zigzags into the Rootabaga Country.
readings.context: Recap: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. Gimme the Ax sold everything and took his son Please Gimme and his daughter Ax Me No Questions on a train that runs to where the railroad tracks go off into the sky. Stilts are long poles to walk on; a handspring, cartwheel and somersault are ways of tumbling.

excerpt.locator: “How They Broke Away to Go to the Rootabaga Country,” from the balloon pickers to the end; opens “Next they came to the country of the balloon pickers. Hanging down from the sky strung on…”; closes “…if the ticket agent wipes sleep from his eyes and asks, “So far? So early? So soon?””.

questions.prompt: How do the balloon pickers reach the balloons, and what happens when a baby picker falls?
facilitatorNotes: They walk on stilts, short ones for low balloons and tall ones for high ones; a baby picker who falls is held up in the air by the balloons in his hand.
evidence: The balloon pickers were walking on high stilts picking balloons.
the handful of balloons they were holding kept them in the air

questions.prompt: Why has one picker floated up into the sky, and when will he come down?
facilitatorNotes: He was singing too happily; his songs made him so light that the balloons pulled him off his stilts. He will come down when his songs are gone and his heart gets heavy.
evidence: He was singing too happy
his heart will get heavy when his songs are all gone

questions.prompt: Tell how a clown is made in the clown country.
facilitatorNotes: It is baked in an oven, set against a fence like a doll, has white fire thrown over it and a red wind pumped through its mouth, and then it jumps away turning cartwheels.
evidence: One man threw a bucket of white fire over it.
The second man pumped a wind pump with a living red wind through the red mouth.

questions.prompt: At the end the story talks straight to you, the listener. What does it tell you to do, and why might Sandburg end that way?
facilitatorNotes: It gives directions for going to the Rootabaga Country yourself: sell everything, and ask for the same ticket. It invites the listener into the game. Some children will say it is a joke; others that it makes the place feel real.
evidence: And if you start to go to that country remember first you must sell everything you have

readings.title: How the Five Rusty Rats Helped Find a New Village
readings.challenge: Follow a story inside a story inside a story.
readings.focus: A gray rat comes in from a blizzard, and Wing Tip the Spick tells her uncles why the people of her village honor rats.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. Wing Tip the Spick comes from the Village of Cream Puffs and is visiting her four uncles in the Village of Liver-and-Onions. A blizzard is a heavy snowstorm with strong wind; a statue stands in a public square to remember something.
readings.contentNote: “Wing Tip the Spick” is one of Sandburg’s nonsense names; the same sound, usually spelled “spic,” is an offensive slur for Spanish-speaking people, and nothing in the story links the two. In the grandfather’s tale, people lost in a blizzard expect to die.

excerpt.locator: “How the Five Rusty Rats Helped Find a New Village,” the whole story; opens “One day while Wing Tip the Spick was visiting her four uncles in the Village of…”; closes “…nice you will feel like going up and taking hold of them to see what will happen to you.””.

questions.prompt: Why do the uncles stop being rude to the gray rat and let him in?
facilitatorNotes: Wing Tip begs them, “in the name of the five rusty rats,” and when they look into her eyes they cannot say no.
evidence: in the name of the five rusty rats, the five lucky rats of the Village of Cream Puffs, please don’t

questions.prompt: What birthday present did her grandfather give her, and how does it work?
facilitatorNotes: Red slippers with a gold clock on each. One runs fast, for when she wants to be early; one runs slow, for when she wants to be late.
evidence: One of the clocks ran fast. The other clock ran slow.

questions.prompt: How did the five rusty rats save the people of Cream Puffs?
facilitatorNotes: They put their noses down in the snow so their long curved tails stuck up like handles; the lost people held on and were led to the place for their new village.
evidence: their long curved tails stuck up far above the snow

questions.prompt: The story begins and ends with a rat and a blizzard. Why do you think Wing Tip wanted her uncles to be kind to the gray rat?
facilitatorNotes: Long ago rats helped her people through a blizzard, so her village honors them; now a rat needs help in a blizzard, and she wants the kindness returned. Some children may say she just loves animals.
evidence: Snow filled the sky and the wind blew and made a noise like heavy wagon axles grinding and crying.
It was the rusty rats who saved their lives

readings.title: The Potato Face Blind Man Who Lost the Diamond Rabbit on His Gold Accordion
readings.challenge: Hear two different explanations for the same thing.
readings.focus: A blind street musician explains why his golden accordion with its diamond rabbits has grown plain and worn.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. The Potato Face Blind Man plays a worn accordion for coins on the corner nearest the post office in the Village of Liver-and-Onions. This is the first of five stories about him. A pawnshop lends money for things left there; 18 carat gold is very fine gold; “Attaboy” means “Well done.”
readings.contentNote: Like everyone in the Rootabaga Country, the blind musician goes by a nonsense name; the stories treat him with respect, but children may want to talk about it.

excerpt.locator: “The Potato Face Blind Man Who Lost the Diamond Rabbit on His Gold Accordion,” the whole story; opens “There was a Potato Face Blind Man used to play an accordion on the Main Street corner…”; closes “…and everybody that don’t get a letter stops and remembers the Potato Face Blind Man.””.

questions.prompt: What did the accordion used to look like?
facilitatorNotes: Gold all over the outside, with a rabbit made of diamonds next to the handles on each side.
evidence: it was gold all over on the outside
a diamond rabbit next to the handles on each side

questions.prompt: What does Any Ice Today think happened to it?
facilitatorNotes: That it was stolen and pawned again and again until the gold wore off.
evidence: somebody stole it and took it to a pawnshop and took it out and somebody stole it again

questions.prompt: What is the Potato Face Blind Man’s own explanation?
facilitatorNotes: Sad music takes the gold away, and each time he plays a sleepy song and falls asleep, another part of the diamond rabbit is gone.
evidence: when they are sad the gold goes away off the accordion
I wake up and the diamond ear of the diamond rabbit is gone

questions.prompt: He says the accordion “knows more knowledge than it used to know.” What could an old, worn accordion know?
facilitatorNotes: It has played many songs and been through hard times, as he has; it has lost its shine but gained experience. Some children may say he is making the best of being poor.
evidence: It knows more knowledge than it used to know just the same as this Potato Face Blind Man knows more knowledge than he used to know.

readings.title: How the Potato Face Blind Man Enjoyed Himself on a Fine Spring Morning
readings.challenge: Find the joke, and then find the serious idea inside the joke.
readings.focus: The Potato Face Blind Man explains to Pick Ups why he hangs a thimble, a cup, a bottomless mug and a sign on his coat.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. The Potato Face Blind Man plays a worn accordion for coins on the corner nearest the post office in the Village of Liver-and-Onions. Flummywisters and yisters are Sandburg’s made-up words. A thimble covers a finger when sewing; galvanized iron is coated so it will not rust; aluminum is a light metal.

excerpt.locator: “How the Potato Face Blind Man Enjoyed Himself on a Fine Spring Morning,” the whole story; opens “On a Friday morning when the flummywisters were yodeling yisters high in the elm trees,…”; closes “…flummywisters sing when they button loose the winter underwear of the baby flummywisters.”.

questions.prompt: What does he hang on his coat buttons, and what does he put beside him on the sidewalk?
facilitatorNotes: A thimble, a tin copper cup and a wooden mug on his buttons; a washtub and a dishpan on the sidewalk; and a sign on his sleeve.
evidence: On the top button of his coat he hung a little thimble.

questions.prompt: What is the wooden mug with no bottom for? Is that funny, kind, or both?
facilitatorNotes: For very poor people who want to give him a nickel and still get it back. It is a joke, but it also lets poor people feel generous.
evidence: It is for the very poor people who wish to give me a nickel and yet get the nickel back.

questions.prompt: Why does his sign say, “I Am Blind Too”?
facilitatorNotes: For people who have eyes but see nothing: they rush to the post office and forget why they came. He calls them his blind brothers.
evidence: they have eyes—but they see nothing with their eyes
They are my blind brothers.

questions.prompt: What do you think it means to have eyes but see nothing? Who in this story sees well?
facilitatorNotes: Not noticing what is around you, like the singing flummywisters or a man playing music. The blind man notices the birds and the song; Pick Ups notices and asks. Children may name people they know who notice a lot.
evidence: they forget why they came and they do not know how to come away

readings.title: Poker Face the Baboon and Hot Dog the Tiger
readings.challenge: Fill a gap the story leaves open, and give your reasons.
readings.focus: Two quiet animal mascots sit beside the Potato Face Blind Man, and a wheelbarrow of silver dollars arrives.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. The Potato Face Blind Man plays a worn accordion for coins on the corner nearest the post office in the Village of Liver-and-Onions. He keeps a washtub and a dishpan beside him in case people ever want to pour out their money. A mascot is a luck bringer; a patent clothes wringer squeezes water from washing; a chauffeur drives someone else’s car.

excerpt.locator: “Poker Face the Baboon and Hot Dog the Tiger,” the whole story; opens “When the moon has a green rim with red meat inside and black seeds on the red meat, then…”; closes “…sky with a green rim and red meat inside and black seeds making spots on the red meat.”.

questions.prompt: What is a Watermelon Moon?
facilitatorNotes: A moon with a green rim and red meat inside with black seeds, like a slice of watermelon; when it shines, people look for anything to happen.
evidence: When the moon has a green rim with red meat inside and black seeds on the red meat

questions.prompt: What does Whitson Whimble see in the animals’ eyes? What does the sign tell him?
facilitatorNotes: Something faraway in the baboon’s eyes, something hungry in the tiger’s. The sign says the blind man can only feel their hair, not see what their eyes say.
evidence: In the eyes of Poker Face was something faraway. In the eyes of Hot Dog was something hungry.
You watch what their eyes say; I can only feel their hair.

questions.prompt: The story never says who sent the man with the wheelbarrow. Who do you think it was? Why?
facilitatorNotes: Most children will say Whitson Whimble, the rich man who stopped, looked, and drove on fifteen minutes before. Others may say the mascots’ luck did it. Both use the order of events.
evidence: Fifteen minutes later a man in overalls came down Main Street with a wheelbarrow.

questions.prompt: The mascots leave a note: “Mascots never stay long.” Why might luck bringers not stay?
facilitatorNotes: Luck comes and goes; if it stayed it would not be luck. Some children will feel sad; others will say the blind man got what he needed.
evidence: Mascots never stay long.

readings.title: The Toboggan-to-the-Moon Dream of the Potato Face Blind Man
readings.challenge: Notice how one person can find the same season sad and not sad.
readings.focus: On an October morning the Potato Face Blind Man tells the dream of a moon toboggan he first had when he could see.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. The Potato Face Blind Man plays a worn accordion for coins on the corner nearest the post office in the Village of Liver-and-Onions. A toboggan is a long sled. Snizzling and sniffering are Sandburg’s own words; hazel nuts are small round nuts.

excerpt.locator: “The Toboggan-to-the-Moon Dream of the Potato Face Blind Man,” the whole story; opens “One morning in October the Potato Face Blind Man sat on the corner nearest the postoffice.”; closes “…white spiders fixed it that way when they snizzled and sniffered and made the toboggan.””.

questions.prompt: Why does Any Ice Today say October is a sad time? What does the blind man answer?
facilitatorNotes: The leaves dry and fall and fill the sky like birds who forget their songs. The blind man says it is “sad and not sad.”
evidence: It is sad and not sad

questions.prompt: Who made the moon toboggan, and who slides down it?
facilitatorNotes: The big white spiders on the moon wove it; the White Gold Boys and Blue Silver Girls slide down it.
evidence: they were weaving a long toboggan, a white toboggan

questions.prompt: What happens when he tries to close his hand and keep the moon children?
facilitatorNotes: They jump out between his fingers, leaving only a little gold and silver dust on his thumb.
evidence: they would snizzle and sniffer and jump out of the cracks between my fingers

questions.prompt: He first had this dream “when I had my eyes, before my luck changed.” Why might falling leaves bring the dream back to him?
facilitatorNotes: Five weeks after the leaves fall the snow comes, and the white toboggan is like snow; the season reminds him of something lovely from when he could see. Some children may hear sadness; others comfort.
evidence: It came to me first when I was a boy, when I had my eyes, before my luck changed.
for every black leaf there will be a thousand snow crystals shining white

readings.title: The Story of Blixie Bimber and the Power of the Gold Buckskin Whincher
readings.challenge: Find the rule a magic object follows, and test it against each new name.
readings.focus: A girl who looks for luck finds a lucky charm with a power that makes her fall in love with every man with an X in his name.
readings.context: Carl Sandburg, a poet from Illinois, made up these stories for his young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, a prairie land of nonsense names and villages. A whincher is Sandburg’s made-up word for a lucky charm, and buckskin is soft deer leather. To keep steady company is to go out together; a steeplejack climbs tall towers to mend them; high jinks are lively fun; a cistern is a tank that collects rain water; the blues are a sad feeling.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of Blixie Bimber and the Power of the Gold Buckskin Whincher,” the whole story; opens “Blixie Bimber grew up looking for luck. If she found a horseshoe she took it home and put…”; closes “…Or it will do other strange things because different whinchers have different powers.”.

questions.prompt: Name two things Blixie does to look for luck.
facilitatorNotes: She hangs up horseshoes with ribbons, looks at the moon over her right shoulder but never her left, watches for the ground hog, and believes her dreams tell the future.
evidence: If she found a horseshoe she took it home and put it on the wall of her room with a ribbon tied to it.

questions.prompt: What is the whincher’s rule? Count the X’s in each man’s name.
facilitatorNotes: The first man with an X, then two X’s, then three: Silas Baxby, Fritz Axenbax, James Sixbixdix. The names grow funnier as the X’s add up.
evidence: The first man you meet with an X in his name
The next man you meet with two X’s in his name

questions.prompt: What does Blixie say each time her relatives ask why she goes with someone?
facilitatorNotes: “It’s a power”; she can’t help it. She doesn’t know the power is in the whincher, not in the man.
evidence: It’s a power—I can’t help myself.

questions.prompt: When the whincher falls into the cistern, whom does Blixie call, and what does that show?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmy the Flea, who whistles her blues away and has no X in his name. Without the charm she goes back to the friend she really liked. Some children may say losing the “luck” was the luckiest thing that happened to her.
evidence: The other was to Jimmy the Flea, the climber, the steeplejack.
Come on over—I got the blues and I want you to whistle ’em away
